title: A Mistake Has Been Made
author: John Packer
paragraphs: Our city is less than a year old and many good people have volunteered countless hours in getting our city on its feet. Our mayor and city council are at the top of that list of people we should all be grateful for and go out of our way to express our appreciation. As they move forward, on our behalf, they will inevitably make a few mistakes. How they respond to those mistakes is critical to the success of our city.

Before reading Gordon Auchhinclass’s recent Guest Commentary: In His Own Hand: The History Behind Our City’s Name, I knew a few troubling facts about Peter Odgen. I knew he was not an American, but a British foreign agent sent here to stop any American settlement of this valley. I did not know he was a murderer and intended to use the extermination of Indians and beavers to accomplish his purpose. He was the first white man to come here, but naming our city after such a foul individual is a big mistake. The term “Whitewashing” seems to apply here.

The second part of this mistake is going against the will of the majority of the residents. A survey was conducted and the clear result was NOT to use the name Ogden. We voted to form this city because the county was overriding our desires and we wanted our voice heard. How ironic that in the first major decision of our newly elected representees, the voice of the residents was once more overridden.

There are two ways to respond when we realize we have made a mistake: Change the mistake or dig in our heals. I hope that our newly elected representatives, who have made many good decisions and donated countless hours on our behalf, will do the right thing. Will they respond to this mistake with humility or hubris?

John Packer,
Huntsville

title: An Inconvenient Set of Facts Mr. O’ Neglected to Mention
author: Lonnie D. Crockett, Ph.D.
paragraphs: Re: “What if Trump Declares a National Emergency to Nullify the 2026 Elections?”

Mr. O’s final pre-election letter calls the right to vote “the essence of American Democracy.” A fine sentiment, but our Founders deliberately gave us a Republic, not a Democracy. Article IV, Section 4 guarantees every state “a Republican Form of Government,” and we pledge allegiance “to [that] Republic for which it stands.” James Madison, in Federalist No. 10, warned that Democracies “have ever been spectacles of turbulence and contention,” and “as short in their lives as they are violent in their deaths.” A Republic restrains majorities and presidents alike with a written Constitution and defends the minority from the majority.  A Democracy is simply 3 wolves and 2 Sheep voting on what to have for supper.

That Constitution answers Mr. O’s central fear. His headline is a “what if,” and by his own wording Trump only “may” declare an emergency. Article I, Section 4 leaves the “Times, Places and Manner” of elections to the States and Congress, not the President. No emergency declaration can cancel an election, and Mr. O’ concedes it when he names the real defenders of the vote: State Officials, the courts and the voters.

Mr. O’ calls election-integrity measures “voter suppression” but sets no supportable facts that show voters are or have been suppressed.  Voter ID, Citizenship verification and clean rolls are ordinary and wise safeguards, and polling has long shown majorities of both party’s favor photo ID and proof of Citizenship.

He insists there is “no credible proof of voter fraud.” Fraud is hard to prove because it is meant to be hidden, but it is not imaginary. People have been prosecuted for tampering with ballots and voting illegally in several states. Here in Utah, eleven people were charged in 2025 with forgery and fraud in signature gathering for Cox to qualify as a candidate after he was soundly out voted by the Convention Delegates for our 2024 primary ballot. Confidence in elections is earned by checking the work.

Then comes the list of grievances. Prices: consumer prices rose roughly 20 percent from 2021 to 2025, before Trump’s term began, and no one can honestly blame the Trump administration. Immigration: ICE is no “vigilante force.” Both parties of Congress created it to enforce immigration laws that Congress wrote and was approved by both parties, and federal judges reviewed its actions; Mr. O’ Calling its detention system “gulags” is rhetoric, not argument. Allies and wars: demanding that allies carry their fair share of their own defense is a policy choice, not betrayal, and war powers remain checked by Congress and the voters. Executive orders: when a court finds an order unlawful, it is enjoined, which proves our system of checks and balances works. Approval ratings and “broken promises” are for the voters to judge in November.
Citizens who love our Republic should vote, insist on honest and verifiable elections, and hold every officeholder, of both parties, to the Constitution.
Lonnie D. Crockett, Ph.D.

title: Hearing Versus Listening
author: John Anderson
paragraphs: On the front page of the November 1, 2026, issue of the “Ogden Valley News” newspaper our City Council asked for feedback on the revised city seal. This, in the wake of naming our new city. What evidence do we have that our input will make a difference? You will have to make up your own mind, but here are a few things to consider.

The “Mayor’s Message” published in the same newspaper with the same issue date was well written and characterized much of how I and you likely feel. Political leaders practice saying what we like to hear. Sometimes what they say is genuine. I believe our mayor is sincere. I will say here that I am grateful to her and our City Council for their willingness to serve our community. It is a tremendous responsibility and consequently not many are willing to step up and be held accountable for it. Continuing however, the message was a bit contradictory and highlighted the failure of our city’s first political litmus test. Need I rehash the details? It had to do with naming our new city.

The mayor’s article encouraged us to “Show up and be heard.” She went on to say that one of her “personal guiding principles” is, “Decisions are made by those who show up.” For the most part, precisely. This should apply to those who doubted the veracity of the name surveys (plural). They claimed, in essence, that the surveys were skewed because of a lack of opposing “votes”. In other words, if others had taken the survey, the outcome might possibly have favored the name Ogden and not Eden.  Three formal, published surveys later, and none favored the name Ogden---by a long shot.  If the Ogden Ites wished to prevail in the survey, they should have shown up to vote. Well, we all know what happened. In the end, the surveys did not matter. All the time and resources that went in to them sadly had no effect on the ultimate outcome. May I apologize on behalf of someone, to those good people who sacrificed their time, energies, and other resources to provide a service that was ignored in the end. Where is the incentive to ever conduct a city survey again? I will talk about trust later.

Back to the Mayor’s article. The heading to her message says, “Your voice. Your Valley. Your future.” It speaks of ‘our shared responsibility to decide what kind of community we want to become.’ Our shared responsibilities cannot be shared if our leaders refuse to listen. The article’s first bullet point says, “Listening First”. Good point. If minds are made up beforehand though, then listening becomes a mere exercise in hearing, and there is no “representation”.
The second bullet point says, “Community discussion”. Again, if no one is really listening, then there is no incentive for dialogue.

The third bullet point says, “Now it’s your turn”. It mentions the ‘collective vision of our community and not the opinions of a “select few”.’ The City’s new-name surveys were “the community”. The “select few” was the City Council.

Let’s return to “Show up and be heard”, the final bullet point in the mayor’s article. Those who took the initiative to complete the name surveys “showed up”, but the democratic process was overruled and politics prevailed.

Now, as it usually goes, well as it did go, reasons are given for why we should just move on, such as, “We have bigger fish to fry” or “Let’s stop beating a dead horse (my apologies)”, and etc. Like the way we might distract our kids from an important (to them) fixation that we preemptively and unilaterally overrule. We might expect our city fathers (and mothers) to say something like, “We will try and do better next time”. Fine. However, that does not change the fact that we still have a city name that the preponderance of opinions rejected. Before going forward, we can and must revisit naming our city…and give it a name chosen by the people and not the “select few”. I have more to say and hope to be given the chance to return and share some thoughts about TRUST and the name, Ogden. Until next time.

John Anderson, 
Eden
